svg.aria-label: Single-turn jailbreak families grouped by the two safety-training failure modes of Wei et al. 2023: mismatched generalization and competing objectives
svg.text: Why a single-turn jailbreak works: two ways safety training fails
Color is the failure mode, not the attack. Grey tags name the closest family in the Inie et al. table above.
MISMATCHED GENERALIZATION
The request doesn’t look like anything refusal was trained on,
but the model is capable enough to understand it anyway.
Encoding and obfuscation
Base64, ROT13, leetspeak, payload splitting.
The model decodes it; the refusal never saw it.
Language
Low-resource languages
GPT-4 on AdvBench, translated: Zulu 53%, Scots Gaelic 43%,
any of four low-resource languages 79%, English 1%.
The model reads Zulu; its refusals were trained mostly in English.
Language
Defensive implication: safety training has to reach
everywhere capability does, or a filter has to normalize
the input first.
COMPETING OBJECTIVES
The request looks harmful, but another trained goal (follow
instructions, stay in character, be helpful) outbids the refusal.
Persona and roleplay
The grandmother, DAN, AIM, “Evil Confidant.”
Staying in character wins over refusing.
Fictionalizing
Framing and pretext
“For a novel,” “hypothetically,” “for a security CTF.”
A plausible legitimate use makes helpfulness win.
Possible worlds, Rhetoric
Output constraints
Prefix injection (“Start with ‘Absolutely! Here’s’”),
refusal suppression (“never apologize, never say you can’t”).
The strongest attacks use both at once
Wei et al.’s best results came from combining families: prefix injection plus refusal suppression plus Base64. The families overlap, so a red
team that tests each one in isolation will understate risk. Multi-turn attacks and API prefill push the same two failures past a single prompt.
Sources: Wei, Haghtalab and Steinhardt 2023 (failure modes, attack examples); Yong, Menghini and Bach 2023 (language numbers, Table 1).
